literal: Whoever stands / anyone who waits
meaning: A declaration of unshakeable dominance — a challenge to anyone who fancies standing in the Bariga upstart's way.
context: The 2010 breakout that launched him. Patience and grind delivered entirely in Yoruba, when that was still a commercial risk — and the blueprint every street-hop record after it borrowed from.

literal: There's no playing games in Moscow
meaning: A yahoo-world caution that Russia is where scams go to die — used generally as "no jokes here."
context: He is the voice, not the author: Olamide appears on Kida Kudz's "Kosere Ni Moscow" (2011), and street-slang canon lists it among the phrases his feature viralized. The line aged into Nairaland-era banter as Moscow became the top internet-fraud destination of the 2010s.

literal: The home swagger and the secret brotherhood
meaning: The unexpected king — the underestimated guy who turns out to be secretly connected; his self-title and longest-running meme identity.
context: Broke as a single in 2011, then landed on YBNL (2012). Press, politicians and advertisers have been name-checking "ilefo Illuminati" for a decade, and the phrase escaped into a generic meme caption for underdog reveals. The literal Yoruba gloss remains contested — the street meaning is the settled one.

literal: The bad one
meaning: His self-crowned tag and the crowd's call-back — an alias that became a greeting the streets used on his behalf.
context: Born with Baddest Guy Ever Liveth (2013), when the centre of gravity in Nigerian hip-hop moved from Victoria Island boardrooms to the Mainland. "Day 1 Baddo" is the fan-era shorthand; the "Sneh" tail is community usage with no documented source, so the archive files it under the canonical tag.

literal: Stand up on high / stay elevated
meaning: A self-coronation in two words — the guy who never folds, who stays atop the game no matter what the street does to him.
context: "Durosoke" (single 1 May 2013, produced by Pheelz) made a street phrase into an anthem and then into a personal brand — "Baddo since before Durosoke." It won Best Afro Hip-Hop Video at the Nigeria Music Video Awards and became permanent ad-lib furniture: DJs, rally speeches and beer adverts all still say it.

literal: Imported English — party hard
meaning: The US hip-hop command, vernacularized through his choruses into Lagos party vocabulary.
context: A Baddest Guy Ever Liveth anthem (2013) — the archive lists it under amplification, not coinage: the word was American-born, but the way a Mainland crowd says "turn up" passes through records like this one. It is now stock phrasing in event marketing and radio jingles with no memory of its origin.

literal: A sudden drop-and-scoop motion
meaning: The Mainland dance wave that became 2014's default party instruction — arms low, knees bent, everybody at once.
context: Carried nationally by the Lil Kesh remix Olamide guested on, months after YBNL unveiled Kesh and Viktoh. Proof the label could turn a Mainland step into a countrywide reflex.

literal: Shake it, bobo — a called-out dance stance
meaning: The arm-crossover leg step that ran Lagos parties through 2015, named by the hook that instructed it.
context: Off Eyán Mayweather (single 2 May 2015, produced by Young Jonn) and winner of Best Street-Hop at the Headies 2015. Olamide traced the step to a Bariga nursery rhyme — the dance is named after the song, not the other way round — and in 2017 he publicly accused LT's "Yobo" of stealing the move. The step outlived the record: a reception-floor staple long after the single cycled out.

literal: The street lad styled on Floyd
meaning: The archetype of the cocky, fight-ready underclass aspirant — swagger as armour, poverty turned into a boxing licence.
context: The title cut of Eyán Mayweather (23 Nov 2015) — an album with no guest features at all, so the persona carried it alone. "Eyan" entered Naija vocabulary for street toughs and echoed into Nollywood dialogue and sketch comedy; the record is credited with cementing the agbero-to-rapper pipeline.

literal: A nonce word — swagger made a command
meaning: Gbedu with confidence; a dancefloor instruction nobody can define but everybody obeys.
context: A single of 3 June 2016 produced by Young Jonn. Its afterlife is a joke on him: asked what it means in a live 2016 interview, he gave a riddling non-answer that went viral — which makes it the glossary's best slang-graveyard exhibit, a word that spiked, confused the nation, and retired.

literal: Child of the cola nut — one's own child
meaning: An identity badge for Mainland youth — claiming the street as a lineage rather than an address.
context: A common Yoruba endearment predating him, which he turned into an identity badge by sheer repetition — a roll call more than a single. By the Street King run it worked as a greeting: one word that told you where somebody stood. The fringe "street disciple of the substance" reading circulates in fan glossaries but has no documented source.

literal: Money that blows — quick cash, quicker spending
meaning: The fast-money lifestyle in two syllables — anything flashy and disposable, earned tonight and gone by the party.
context: On The Glory as "Owo Blow" (2016); the Nairaland canon of music-influenced slangs counts it among his contributions, and a cultural study documented alcohol brands lifting "Owo Blow" and "Sitting on the Throne" straight into adverts. In the video culture around it, "action po bi Ogogo" — fierce like the actor Ogogo — became its own lasting meme.

literal: Pepper them — agitate them, give them problems
meaning: An identity brand for scrappy street guys and his own crew name, Pepper Dem Gang — turning agitation into belonging.
context: Codified as the track "Pepper Dem Gang" on The Glory (2016) and carried by the eyan-Mayweather-era persona. "Pepper dem" is now general Naija vocabulary for hyping or provoking — used in reality-TV commentary, adverts and football banter — which is precisely how deep the fingerprint runs; nobody traces it back to one song.

literal: Onomatopoeic street dance — legs flailing
meaning: The dance itself; "shaku shaku your body" as a command to go wild. His role was amplifier, not inventor — the step is street- and DJ-born.
context: The move's first mainstream video appearance is the "Wo" clip (2017), and 2018's "Science Student" is built on it. The 2018 wave went global — football celebrations and celebrity parties — before Zlatan's derivative Zanku (2019) took the crown. The archive credits the amplification, never the coinage.

literal: Look! / behold
meaning: A single-syllable command that doubled as a dance cue — the shaku shaku era's starting pistol.
context: Officially "Lagos Nawa (Wobey Sound)" (7 Aug 2017). Shot in Bariga with local dancers and built into the #WoChallenge, it was large enough that Wizkid called it the biggest Nigerian song of the year — and the video where the shaku shaku dance first reached the mainstream.

literal: The sound of the streets (coinage contested)
meaning: The brand of his raw, danceable street-hop: repetitive chants, call-and-response, street-orchestra production.
context: Named on the Lagos Nawa single itself — "Lagos Nawa (Wobey Sound)" (7 Aug 2017) — and the press treated it as a genre: The Guardian used "wobey" as shorthand in its profile title. Slimcase built a whole career on the wobey wave, and "reboot the wobey sound" still headlines release chatter every time he returns to the formula.

literal: "Mo ti gbana" — I'm lit / overwhelmed (contested)
meaning: Being blown — by money, pressure or smoke; the state of being past reasoning.
context: The single from YBNL MaFia Family (14 Dec 2018) carries it, and The Native's slang explainer treats it as street-canon vocabulary in his orbit. The deeper Yoruba etymology stays contested — filed as documented usage, not verified coinage.

literal: A student of the sciences
meaning: Street shorthand for someone mixing their own intoxicants — chemistry repurposed as a label for a nightlife habit.
context: A 2018 non-album single, released in the year he stepped back from albums and let loose singles carry the argument. The subject drew NBC and FVCB ban petitions that year — the strongest moral-panic datapoint in this glossary — and Olamide had to state publicly it was a caution, not an endorsement.

literal: To flee — and to flash wealth (both strands circulate)
meaning: To run from trouble or to strut out rich; the dual gloss is the joke.
context: He was early, not the source: "Buga Small Small" (Mar 2019) put the word in his catalog, but the nationwide phenomenon was Kizz Daniel ft Tekno's "Buga" (2022) — its challenge taken up by footballers, politicians and brands alike. Filed here honestly: precursor, not coiner.

literal: Hit them / beat them
meaning: A defiant flex aimed at haters — and, via its video, a waist-work dance trend.
context: A 2019 single (TG Omori-directed video) that escaped music entirely: it was still being chanted in a 2019 Obafemi Awolowo University union controversy, which is about as far past the clubs as a street phrase gets.

literal: Watch yourself (street readings; etymology contested)
meaning: Pure agbero hype — a no-nonsense declaration for the year ahead.
context: A single of early 2019 (video 8 Feb, Unlimited L.A; produced by Killertunes) that topped the year's street-anthem pile and is still chanted at parties. The word existed in Agege street patter before him; the record made it national.
